title: Demonstrate an understanding of abattoir layout and construction

lessons.title: Layout and product flow
lessons.html:
The principle of forward flow

An abattoir is laid out so that animals, carcasses and products move in one direction only, from the dirtiest areas to the cleanest, without crossing back. This forward (linear) flow is the most important principle of abattoir design. It prevents cross-contamination between live animals, hides, guts and finished meat.

Typical sequence of areas

  1. Off-loading ramps and lairage (including isolation pens for suspect animals)
  2. Stunning and bleeding area
  3. Dirty area: dehiding or skinning (or scalding and de-hairing for pigs), head and feet removal
  4. Clean area: evisceration, inspection, splitting, trimming, washing
  5. Weighing, classification and marking
  6. Chillers and, where present, freezers
  7. Deboning and packing, where present
  8. Dispatch

Separate flows

By-products leave the line through their own routes so they never cross the meat flow:

  • Hides and skins to the hide store
  • Rough offal to the rough offal room; red offal to the red offal room
  • Heads and feet to their processing areas
  • Condemned material to the lockable condemned room
  • Inedible material and blood to rendering or approved disposal

Staff flow

Workers in dirty areas and clean areas should have separate entrances, change rooms or at least clear crossing rules with hand-wash, boot-wash and apron-wash facilities. Colour-coded clothing helps enforce this.

Detention and inspection

Inspection points must be placed so that heads, organs and carcasses are presented together. A detention rail leads off the main line so that suspect carcasses can be removed without stopping the flow.

lessons.title: Planning, design and construction
lessons.html:
Planning an abattoir

Planning starts with key questions: which species, how many animals per day, what market (local, regional, export), what services are available (water, electricity, effluent disposal), and where the animals come from.

Site selection

  • Reliable supply of potable water, and electricity.
  • Ability to treat and dispose of effluent legally.
  • Good road access for livestock trucks and refrigerated trucks.
  • Away from sources of pollution, flooding and dense housing; prevailing winds considered for odours.
  • Room for future expansion.

Construction requirements

ElementRequirement
FloorsImpervious, non-slip, durable, sloping to drains
WallsSmooth, impervious, light coloured, easy to clean; coved joints with floors
CeilingsSmooth, easy to clean, no dripping condensation
DrainsAdequate capacity, trapped, with screens; flow from clean to dirty areas
LightingSufficient intensity, especially at inspection points; shatterproof covers
VentilationRemoves steam, heat and odours; prevents condensation
Doors and openingsSelf-closing where needed, pest-proof, wide enough for rail traffic
RailsHeight suited to species so carcasses never touch the floor

Equipment and facilities

  • Hand-wash basins with non-hand-operated taps and knife sterilizers at every work station.
  • Stainless steel or other approved materials for food-contact surfaces.
  • Pest control measures: screens, bait stations outside, sealed gaps.
  • Ablution and change facilities that do not open directly onto meat areas.
  • Facilities for meat inspection staff.

lessons.title: Statutory requirements and grading of abattoirs
lessons.html:
The legal framework

Abattoirs in South Africa are regulated under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and its regulations. Key requirements include:

  • Abattoirs must be registered with the provincial veterinary authority before they operate.
  • Plans for new abattoirs or major changes must be approved before construction.
  • Structural, hygiene and operational standards set out in the regulations must be met.
  • Meat inspection must be provided by authorised persons.
  • A hygiene management system must be in place, including records.

Other laws apply too, including the Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 for worker safety, the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 for welfare, the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984 for disease control, the National Water Act 36 of 1998 for water use and effluent, and municipal by-laws.

Grading (categories) of abattoirs

Abattoirs are categorised according to their throughput, measured in slaughter units per day, as set out in the regulations. The broad categories are:

  • High throughput abattoirs: larger plants with full facilities and greater structural requirements.
  • Low throughput abattoirs: smaller plants, often serving rural towns, with requirements suited to their size.
  • The regulations also provide for smaller, rural-type facilities with simpler requirements.

The category determines the maximum number of animals that may be slaughtered per day and the facilities required. An abattoir may not exceed its registered throughput. Check the current regulations for the exact unit definitions and limits.

Audits

Provincial veterinary services audit abattoirs. Many abattoirs are scored with a hygiene assessment system, and export abattoirs are also audited against importing countries' standards.

lessons.title: Water use and effluent
lessons.html:
Water in the abattoir

Abattoirs use large amounts of water for washing carcasses, cleaning, sterilizers, scalding, offal processing and staff facilities. All water that comes into contact with meat or food-contact surfaces must be potable, meeting the South African drinking water standard (SANS 241).

  • Hot water must be available for sterilizers and cleaning at the temperatures the regulations and procedures require.
  • Water storage must be protected against contamination; reservoirs are cleaned and water is tested regularly.
  • Non-potable water, if used for limited purposes such as fire-fighting, must be in clearly identified separate pipes that never connect to potable supplies.

Saving water

  • Dry cleaning (removing solids) before washing.
  • Trigger-operated hose nozzles and low-volume, high-pressure cleaning.
  • Repairing leaks promptly and metering water use per area.

Effluent

Abattoir effluent contains blood, fat, manure, ingesta, hair and cleaning chemicals. It has a very high organic load and can severely pollute rivers and groundwater. The National Water Act 36 of 1998 and municipal by-laws control its disposal.

Handling and treatment

  1. Blood recovery: collect blood separately; it is the largest single source of organic load.
  2. Screening: remove hair, paunch contents and solids from drains.
  3. Fat traps: separate fat and grease.
  4. Treatment: depending on size and location, discharge to a municipal sewer under permit, or on-site treatment such as ponds or other approved systems.
  5. Solid waste: manure and paunch contents composted or removed; condemned material rendered or disposed of by approved methods.

Key points

  • Product flows forward from dirty to clean areas, with separate by-product routes.
  • Construction must give impervious, cleanable surfaces, good drainage, lighting and ventilation.
  • Abattoirs must be registered under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and are categorised by throughput.
  • Only potable water may touch meat.
  • Recover blood, screen solids and trap fat to reduce effluent pollution.

quiz.question: What is the most important principle of abattoir layout?

options.text: Forward flow from dirty to clean areas without crossing back
Placing the chiller next to the lairage
Keeping all by-products on the main line
Using as few rooms as possible

quiz.question: On what basis are abattoirs categorised as high or low throughput?

options.text: The size of the parking area

quiz.question: Which is the largest single source of organic load in abattoir effluent?
Which standard must water that contacts meat meet?

options.text: The South African drinking water standard (SANS 241)

quiz.question: Which floor characteristic is required in an abattoir?

options.text: Impervious, non-slip and sloping to drains

quiz.question: An abattoir may slaughter more animals per day than its registered throughput when demand is high.
Non-potable water pipes must never be connected to potable water supplies.
Which are effective steps in handling abattoir effluent? (select all that apply)

options.text: Discharging untreated effluent into the nearest river
Washing paunch contents into the drains
